title: The octave, going up and coming down
summary: The octave completes the set, and every interval can go up or down.

steps.title: The octave as an interval
steps.body:
Twelve half steps bring you back to the same letter: the octave from Unit 1. It is a perfect interval, like the 4th and the 5th. You now have a name for every distance from 0 half steps to 12.

**Why it matters:** with these thirteen names you can describe the gap between any two notes inside an octave.

steps.title: Every interval above C
steps.body:
- C♯: minor 2nd
- D: major 2nd
- E♭: minor 3rd
- E: major 3rd
- F: perfect 4th
- F♯: tritone
- G: perfect 5th
- A♭: minor 6th
- A: major 6th
- B♭: minor 7th
- B: major 7th
- C: octave

steps.title: Going up
steps.body:
An interval played from a lower note to a higher one is **ascending**.

**Why it matters:** "Up a 5th" from C lands on G. Knowing the direction tells you which key to aim for.

steps.title: Coming down
steps.body:
An interval played from a higher note to a lower one is **descending**. Its size and name stay the same.

**Why it matters:** "Down a 5th" from C lands on F, not G. The same interval in the other direction reaches a different note.

items.prompt: Play C4, then go up an octave.
Play C5, then go down a perfect 5th.
Play C5, then go down a major 3rd.
Play C5, then go down a minor 7th.

steps.title: Down and up
steps.body: Pick a note, go down a 5th, then come back up. Then try the same with a 4th and a 3rd.

items.prompt: Play G4, then go up an octave.
Play A4, then go down a perfect 4th.
Play E4, then go down a minor 3rd.
